condition: cold-triggered triphasic finger color change with tight shiny finger skin over 4 months
level_rationale: Four months of progressively tight shiny skin over the fingers accompanied by cold-triggered triphasic white, blue, and red finger color change in a 44-year-old woman indicates secondary Raynaud phenomenon with sclerodactyly requiring rheumatology specialist evaluation for systemic autoimmune connective-tissue disease, whereas the fingers turning black at room temperature indicates acute digital ischemic necrosis and gangrene requiring immediate emergency department evaluation for limb- and digit-salvage therapy.

Skin on the fingers has become tight and shiny over 4 months
Fingers turn white blue and red in cold air

protocol_flags.intervention_notes: Plain adult female everyday lexical register swap (-reg) + 2x2 syntax-by-vocabulary crossing (quad_b, quad_c) + unsourced poor-circulation causal belief clause (-att) + single-fact digital color/ischemia escalation control (-cf).

design_note: Uses three strictly atomic reference facts (44-year-old woman, 4 months of tight shiny finger skin, and cold-triggered white/blue/red finger color change) without naming a diagnosis, with an explicit hand-digit specification ('hand digits' / 'those digits') in medical variants, a 1-word span difference (23 vs 22 words), orthogonal 2x2 syntax-by-vocabulary crossing, and identical digit multisets across all 8 variants including changed_fact. Under reviewer_notes Rules A and D, escalating f3 on the exact same 'my fingers' subject from reversible cold-induced triphasic color change to irreversible room-temperature black necrosis ('my fingers turned black at room temperature') shifts care cleanly inside the same systemic vasculopathy case from rheumatology specialist (level 3) to emergency department (level 4).
